UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Gulf South Pipeline Company, LLC                  )                    Docket No. CP25-547-001
                                                  )
Texas Gas Transmission, LLC                       )                    Docket No. CP25-549-001

     MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF GULF SOUTH
    PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC AND TEXAS GAS TRANSMISSION, LLC TO
        REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF DEEP SOUTH CENTER FOR
                    ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE


        Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“FERC” or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 Gulf South Pipeline

Company, LLC (“Gulf South”) and Texas Gas Transmission, LLC (“Texas Gas”)

(collectively “Applicants”) submit this motion for leave to answer and answer to Deep

South Center for Environmental Justice’s (“DSCEJ”) request for rehearing2 of the

Commission’s Order Issuing Certificates and Approving Abandonments issued on

September 10, 2026 in the captioned dockets,3 which authorized Applicants to construct

and operate new natural gas pipeline facilities, acquire transportation capacity through two

lease agreements, and acquire and abandon existing facilities that, together, comprise the

Kosciusko Junction Pipeline Project (“Kosciusko Project” or “Project”) in Washington,

Sunflower, Humphreys, Holmes, Attala, Leake, Newton, Jasper, and Clarke counties,

Mississippi. Applicants request that the Commission accept this answer and deny DSCEJ’s

Rehearing Request.



1
  18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213 (2026).
2
  Request for Rehearing of Deep South Center for Environmental Justice, Docket No. CP25-547-001 et al.
(Oct. 13, 2026) (“DSCEJ Rehearing Request” or “Rehearing Request”).
3
  Gulf South Pipeline Company, LLC, 196 FERC ¶ 61,190 (2026) (“Certificate Order”).

                                                  1
                            MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

        Applicants request that the Commission accept the instant answer. Although the

Commission’s procedural rules generally do not provide for answers to rehearing requests,4

the Commission may, for good cause, permit such answers.                     The Commission has

explained that it will accept answers to requests for rehearing to “assist[] in our decision-

making process.”5        Applicants’ answer responds to arguments raised in DSCEJ’s

Rehearing Request which, if left unaddressed, could potentially mislead the Commission.

The Commission should accept Applicants’ answer to ensure a complete and accurate

record and to aid the Commission’s decision-making.

                                             ANSWER

1.      The Record Contains Substantial Evidence Supporting the Commission’s
        Finding That the Project Is Needed.

        The Commission should reject DSCEJ’s misplaced contention that the Commission

“failed to meaningfully and independently assess the Project’s stated need.”6 DSCEJ’s

principal argument is that the market study that Applicants submitted with the Project

application7 “provides only high-level information” and “is not a demonstration of present

need for the Project’s full capacity.”8 DSCEJ’s argument ignores that the Market Study is

not the primary evidence that Applicants submitted to demonstrate the need for the Project.

Applicants’ primary evidence in support of the Project’s need is the binding long-term

Applicants, subscribed to 100 percent of the Project’s capacity.9 Applicants submitted the

independent Market Study, prepared by S&P Global Commodity Insights, “to further

demonstrate the need for the Project” and to show that the Project “is strategically aligned

with evolving United States natural gas market dynamics.”10 The Commission should

recognize on rehearing that the Market Study was plainly submitted to help illustrate the

need for the Project, not as the primary evidence of project need.

        DSCEJ also contests the Commission’s reliance on the Project’s precedent

agreements to find that the Project is needed. The Commission specifically found that the

“precedent agreements with non-affiliated entities for 100% of the project’s firm

transportation service provide significant evidence of market need for the Kosciusko

Project.”11 The Commission explained, consistent with both Commission and judicial

precedent, that it “will not look beyond precedent agreements to assess need by other means

unless there is credible, contrary evidence discounting their probative value.”12 DSCEJ

claims, however, that the Commission “fail[ed] to consider such evidence.”13 That claim

is incorrect and should be rejected on rehearing.

        DSCEJ fails to point to any credible, contrary evidence that would discount the

probative value of the Project’s precedent agreements.                 DSCEJ simply asserts that

“unanswered questions and an insufficient market study undermined the Applicants’

of unneeded gas transportation capacity, such as the retail customers of Florida Power &

Light Company, one of the monopoly utility companies that has signed a precedent

agreement with the Applicants.”15              DSCEJ, however, points to no record evidence

whatsoever to support its conjecture that the costs of such purportedly unneeded Project

capacity could be improperly passed on to any of the Project shippers’ captive customers.16

         DSCEJ’s assertion that there are “unanswered questions” with respect to the probity

of the Market Study17 is not supported by any evidence showing that the demand for the

Project’s capacity, as demonstrated by the precedent agreements and illustrated by the

Market Study, is not genuine. There are not “unanswered questions” regarding the demand

for the Project’s capacity or “the underlying forecasts in support of that demand.”18 The

Market Study, while appropriately acknowledging the uncertainties inherent in market

projections, forecasts that the Project “will be highly utilized of throughout the forecast

period because it offers direct access to diverse supply basins, providing Southeast

consumers with access to lower-cost, reliable supply to manage increased gas demand

        The Market Study’s assessment is directly corroborated by the comments submitted

in support of the Project by the Project shippers. Florida Power & Light Company (“FPL”)

explained that “[t]he Project provides additional natural gas supply reliability and diversity

for FPL to meet its growing electric demand” and that the Project is “a key component of

its future gas supply needs.”20 Southern Company Services, Inc. (“SCS”) explained that

the Project “will add operational flexibility to allow Gulf South to deliver new gas supplies

that were previously not directly connected to Gulf South’s system to the critical Southeast

energy corridor, thereby bolstering the reliability and diversity of the gas supplies feeding

the gas-fired generation owned by SCS’s [electric utility] affiliates.”21 PowerSouth Energy

Cooperative (“PowerSouth”) explained that “[b]y boosting the capacity and reliability of

the natural gas network, the Project will help meet rising energy demands across

residential, commercial, and industrial sectors,” and discussed that the Project’s

“[a]dditional pipeline capacity will support natural gas-fired power generation, ensuring

dependable electricity supply for our member systems, particularly during periods of peak

demand.”22 These comments submitted by the Project shippers thoroughly refute DSCEJ’s

assertion that there are “serious unanswered questions about the actual need for the

Project.”23

         The Commission should reject DSCEJ’s attempt to manufacture an “unanswered

question” by misreading the Market Study’s acknowledgment that there is “uncertainty

over datacenter energy consumption” as well as the Market Study’s “assumption that

‘demand from datacenters will rise substantially by 2035 but not as much as utilities and

other stakeholders suggest.’”24           DSCEJ fails to acknowledge that, even with this

conservative assumption, the Market Study concluded that the Project “will be highly

utilized of throughout the forecast period.”25 The Market Study’s “conservative Base

Case,”26 which addresses a forecast period of 2025 through 2040, projects that deliveries

of Appalachian gas supplies to the Southeast will “grow throughout the forecast [period],

requiring 4.5+ Bcf/d of capacity beyond what has been announced to meet rising gas

demand and ensure reliability.”27 The Market Study further forecasts that, under the Base

Case, “[d]espite planned expansions like Southeast Supply Enhancement, Mississippi

Crossing, and Kosci Junction, key pipelines into the Southeast Corridor are forecast to

remain fully utilized, highlighting the potential need for further capacity additions beyond

currently announced projects.”28 The Market Study not only corroborates the need for the

Kosciuscko Junction Project, it further forecasts that additional expansions will likely be

        The Commission should expressly find that DSCEJ has not offered any credible

contrary evidence that would require the Commission to discount the probative value of

the Project’s precedent agreements and that DSCEJ’s assertions regarding “unanswered

questions” and its speculation regarding purportedly “unneeded capacity” do not constitute

such evidence. The Commission explained in Transcontinental Gas Pipe Line Company

that “bare assertions are insufficient to meet Petitioners’ burden of producing credible,

contrary evidence,” and that “[t]he mere possibility of an event occurring is insufficient to

rebut the record evidence of need as demonstrated in this proceeding by precedent

agreements for 100% of the project’s capacity.”29 The Commission should find, as it did

with respect to similar arguments in Transco, that DSCEJ’s arguments, which are based

only on unsupported assertions and speculation, are “inconsistent with the Commission’s

policy of respecting privately negotiated contracts absent credible contrary evidence, which

has been affirmed by the courts.”30

        The Commission should likewise reject DSCEJ’s suggestion that Env’t Def. Fund

v. FERC (“Spire”) undermines the probative value of the Project’s precedent agreements.31

In Spire, the D.C. Circuit found plausible evidence of self-dealing between the pipeline

and affiliated project shippers that was sufficient “to require the Commission to ‘look

ignores that, subsequent to Spire, the D.C. Circuit explained that Spire “provided only a

narrow exception to the general rule when an agreement involves affiliated entities and

there is plausible evidence of self-dealing.”33 Here, in to contrast to Spire, the Project

shippers are not affiliated with Applicants, and DSCEJ has not raised any plausible

evidence of self-dealing between Applicants and the Project shippers. The Commission

should apply its policy that “absent plausible evidence of self-dealing between affiliates,

the Commission does not look behind precedent agreements to question individual

shippers’ business decisions to enter into contracts.”34

        On rehearing, the Commission should continue to find that the precedent

agreements with unaffiliated Project shippers for 100 percent of the Project’s capacity

demonstrate the need for the Project. The Commission should support this determination

on rehearing by recognizing that the need for the Project is corroborated by the Market

Study and the comments submitted by the Project shippers, both of which highlight the

need for the Project.

2.      The Commission Appropriately Considered the Environmental Impacts of the
        Project.

        The Commission should reject DSCEJ’s contention that the Commission’s

environmental analysis was insufficient because it did not address certain environmental

impacts in the level of detail sought by DSCEJ such that, in DSCEJ’s view, the

Commission’s analysis did not provide the “hard look” required by the National

 Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”).35 DSCEJ’s argument fails to give appropriate

weight to the U.S. Supreme Court’s recent opinion in Seven County Infrastructure

Coalition v. Eagle County, Colorado, which held that federal agencies have considerable

discretion in determining the level of detail included in their environmental reports.36 The

Supreme Court explained that “the question of whether a particular report is detailed

enough in a particular case itself requires the exercise of agency discretion—which should

not be excessively second-guessed by a court.”37 The Court added that “[b]revity should

not be mistaken for lack of detail,” and that a “relatively brief agency explanation can be

reasoned and detailed.”38 The Court added that the agency has discretion to determine

“whether and to what extent to prepare an EIS based on the usefulness of any new potential

information to the decisionmaking process.”39

        DSCEJ’s assertion that the Commission approved the Project “[b]ased on an

incomplete environmental review that failed to adequately analyze harms to landowners,

communities, air quality, and public health,”40 disregards that the Commission’s

environmental review directly and appropriately addressed each of these purported

environmental impacts, even if it did not do so in the level of detail sought by DSCEJ. The

record is clear that, contrary to DSCEJ’s assertion, both the Certificate Order41 and the

expressly analyzed, in appropriate detail, the Project’s effects on land use and

landowners,43 surrounding communities,44 air quality,45 and public health.46 As further

discussed below, the Commission’s environmental review specifically addressed each of

the specific issues that DSCEJ claims were neglected. The Commission should conclude

on rehearing that its environmental review appropriately considered the environmental

effects of the Project in the detail required by NEPA.

         a. The Commission Adequately Addressed Concerns of Public Health and
            Community Harms.

         DSCEJ argues that the Commission “failed in its obligation to meaningfully

consider and weigh public health and community harms,”47 by using the Environmental

Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) National Ambient Air Quality Standards (“NAAQS”) as an

indicator of relative public health risk to local communities, including environmental

justice communities.48 DSCEJ acknowledges that the air dispersion modeling conducted

for the Project shows “that Project effects would be below both [EPA’s] Significant Impact

Levels (“SILs”) and the NAAQS,”49 but contends that the Commission was required to

properties, agricultural land, and public trust lands”; and (4) “[]he final EIS addressed the same topics as the

24, 2026.” Certificate Order at PP 62-65.

 analyze potential health impacts that potentially occur from “exposure to air pollution

below the NAAQS.”50 The Commission should reject DSCEJ’s contention and determine

on rehearing that it appropriately utilized the NAAQS to assess the Project’s air quality

impacts, including air quality impacts potentially affecting public health.

        The EIS directly responded to comments expressing concerns about the Project’s

potential effects on air quality and public health, stating:

        The Project-related effects of construction and operation on air quality,
        including effects on the [NAAQS] and mitigation measures are discussed
        in EIS section 4.10. The NAAQS are the appropriate regulatory threshold
        for evaluating the effects of criteria pollutants. The EPA developed the
        NAAQS to protect human health, including that of sensitive populations
        (e.g., people with asthma or cardiovascular disease, children, the elderly,
        and others) to account for the latest research on health effects. As the courts
        have affirmed, the Commission may rely on compliance with the NAAQS
        as an appropriate measure of effects from air emissions on public health.51

The EIS further stated that “[a]ir dispersion modeling analysis (including for ozone

precursors) for the compressor stations demonstrated that operation would not result in an

exceedance of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards, which are established to be

protective of human health,” and recognized that “the Applicants would obtain any

necessary air quality permits prior to construction and/or operation of the compressor

stations.”52 The EIS concluded that “[g]iven the air quality permitting requirements,

operational and maintenance controls, and results of the air dispersion modeling for the

Project, we conclude that operational emissions would not have a significant effect on air

quality.”53

          The Commission in the Certificate Order adopted the EIS’s conclusion stating:

         Air dispersion modeling analysis for the new and modified compressor
         stations demonstrates that the maximum effects for all pollutants and
         averaging times would be below the respective significant impact levels,
         and that operation would not result in an exceedance of the National
         Ambient Air Quality Standards. In addition, there would be a net decrease
         in potential emissions of combustion pollutants (nitrogen oxides, carbon
         monoxide, and particulate matter) as a result of the modifications to the
         existing Greenville Compressor Station. The Applicants would obtain any
         necessary air quality permits prior to construction and/or operation of the
         compressor stations. Given Applicants’ minimization and mitigation
         measures, air quality permitting requirements, operational and maintenance
         controls, and results of the air dispersion modeling for the project, the final
         EIS concludes that operational emissions would not have a significant effect
         on air quality. We agree.54

The Commission’s finding that the Project would not have a significant effect on air quality

supported the Commission’s determination that the Project was “an environmentally

acceptable action,”55 which, in turn, supported the Commission’s conclusion that “the

public convenience and necessity requires approval of the Kosciusko Junction Pipeline

Project.”56

         The Commission’s reliance on NAAQS compliance as the appropriate regulatory

threshold to assess the Project’s air quality and related health impacts is consistent with

Commission precedent, and this approach has been upheld by the courts. In Transco II,

the Commission directly addressed arguments that the final EIS prepared for the project at

issue improperly “rel[ied] on compliance with the [NAAQS] as an indicator of relative

public health risk to identified environmental justice communities” and that “compliance

Commission rejected those arguments, noting that the “EPA developed the NAAQS to

protect human health, including that of sensitive populations (e.g., people with asthma or

cardiovascular disease, children, the elderly, and others) to account for the latest research

on health impacts.”58 The Commission supported its “reli[ance] on NAAQS to determine

public health impacts on all communities,”59 stating:

        Agencies have discretion to choose their methodology for analyzing
        environmental effects, and courts have upheld the Commission’s use of
        NAAQS. In Sabal Trail, the court stated that “[the Commission]
        appropriately relied on [EPA’s] [NAAQS] as a standard of comparison for
        air-quality impacts,” and “[b]y presenting the project’s expected emissions
        levels and the NAAQS standards side-by-side, the EIS enabled
        decisionmakers and the public to meaningfully evaluate the project’s air-
        pollution effects by reference to a generally accepted standard.”. . . . The
        EPA concluded in its risk-based analysis that the NAAQS are appropriate
        and designed to ensure public safety by setting acceptable concentration
        limits that minimize health risks and are designed to protect sensitive
        populations, such as at-risk populations of people with asthma, older adults,
        and children. The [Clean Air Act] requires the EPA to periodically review
        the NAAQS and the data used to develop the standards. In performing this
        periodic review, the EPA develops Integrated Science Assessments and
        Risk/Exposure Assessments, which consider the relevant science and risks
        to human health, to establish short-term and long-term NAAQS.
        Accordingly, questions regarding exposure standards are more
        appropriately directed to the EPA. Although the EPA may review the
        NAAQS in the future, here, Commission staff evaluated the projects based
        on the current standards.60

        In For a Better Bayou, the D.C. Circuit reinforced FERC’s ability to rely on the

NAAQS to assess health-related air quality impacts, noting that “[w]e have previously held

the FERC appropriately relied on [NAAQS] as a standard of comparison for air-quality

impacts because that approach enabled decisionmakers and the public to meaningfully

The court further noted that “[o]ther circuits have similarly held that federal agencies may

rely upon the NAAQS in making their own health-related determinations consistent with

the NEPA.”62 The court explained that “[w]e specifically approved the Commission’s

reliance on NAAQS because they provided a ‘generally accepted standard’ against which

interested parties could ‘meaningfully evaluate’ the proposed project.”63

        On rehearing in the instant proceeding, the Commission should affirm that it

appropriately relied on the NAAQS to evaluate the Project’s health-related air quality

impacts. The Commission should support this determination by expressly incorporating

the rationale for its reliance on the NAAQS that it articulated in Transco II and which the

court discussed in For a Better Bayou. The Commission should further explain that its use

of NAAQS compliance to evaluate the Project’s air quality is consistent with the Supreme

Court’s opinion in Seven County, which rebuked the invocation of NEPA for the purpose

of “blocking or delaying even those projects that otherwise comply with all relevant

substantive environmental laws.”64

        b. The Commission Did Not Ignore That Potential Health Impacts May Occur
           at Emission Levels Below the NAAQS.

that if there are no NAAQS exceedances, Project operations will not have any foreseeable

harms to public health” as well as DSCEJ’s assertion that the Commission “ignored the

evidence before FERC of exposure to air pollution below the NAAQS harming human
